title: Trinity Agent Credential Declaration
description: The credential half of an agent's template.yaml: `credentials:` declares WHICH variables the agent needs, and the sibling `credential_setup:` describes each one so an operator can fill it in. Rooted at template.yaml, so validate the whole file against this — the two keys are one contract joined by a mandatory cross-reference, and validating either alone cannot check it. `additionalProperties: true` throughout: template.yaml carries many keys this schema deliberately says nothing about, and a template that predates this schema must stay VALID. This is the authoritative documentation contract; the backend reader (services/template_service.normalize_credential_requirements) is tolerant by design — it degrades and reports named errors rather than rejecting a template, so a file can be non-conforming here and still list in the catalog. Version-stamped $id: a future revision gets a new date, and this one keeps answering for templates written against it.

credentials.description: Which credentials this agent needs, BY NAME ONLY. This key is frozen: it will never accept per-variable objects. An already-deployed older Trinity reads `env_file` and then does `agent_credentials.get(name, "")`, so a list of mappings is a TypeError at the moment it writes the agent's .env — which is why enrichment lives in the sibling `credential_setup:` instead. Absent, null and `{}` all mean the same thing: this agent needs no credentials. That is a first-class, supported state, not an omission.

mcp_servers.description: Per-MCP-server credential declaration. Each key is a server name as it appears in .mcp.json / .mcp.json.template.

env_vars.description: Variable names this server needs. Names only — each entry MUST be a string. An entry that is a mapping or a list is the single most common way to break a credential reader.

env_file.description: Variable names written to the agent's .env. Names only — one string per list item. A bare string here (`env_file: OPENAI_API_KEY`) is iterated CHARACTER BY CHARACTER by older readers, writing `O=`, `P=`, `E=` and never the real credential.

config_files.description: DEPRECATED — do not use in new templates. Writes a rendered file into the agent's credential directory at creation time, with `{VAR}` placeholders substituted. `path` MUST be relative to that directory with no `..` segment (the backend rejects an absolute or traversing path at the boundary AND re-checks containment at the write sink; 26 escape attempts including URL-encoded, full-width and UNC forms were verified to escape zero times). Enumerated here rather than left undocumented ON PURPOSE: this artifact is the authoritative contract, and a contract that silently answers VALID to `path: /etc/cron.d/pwn` blesses a traversal. Undocumented is not a control against an author who knows the key — only against the reviewer who does not. Retained for backward compatibility with templates that already use it.

path.description: Destination path, RELATIVE to the agent's credential directory. No leading `/`, no `..` segment.

template.description: File contents, with `{VAR_NAME}` placeholders substituted from the agent's credentials.

credential_setup.description: OPTIONAL per-variable setup guidance. It DECORATES the variables `credentials:` declares — it cannot declare them. Every entry's `name` MUST appear in `credentials.mcp_servers.<server>.env_vars` or `credentials.env_file`; an entry naming anything else is reported as a named error and DROPPED (its valid siblings survive). That cross-reference is what makes a sibling key safe: two keys describe the same variable, and only one of them can introduce it, so they cannot drift. Absent means the agent's credentials are un-enriched, which is valid — every normalized record then carries `required: "unknown"`.

name.description: The variable this entry describes. MUST be declared in `credentials:`.

title.description: Short human-facing label, e.g. "Stripe secret key". Defaults to `name`. Author-controlled text that reaches an operator-facing checklist, so the backend strips non-printable characters from it.

description.description: One or two sentences on what this credential is for and what it lets the agent do. This is the field an operator reads while deciding whether to hand over a key.

required.description: Whether the agent needs this credential to function. Omitting it on an ENRICHED entry means `true` — an author who took the trouble to describe a variable meant it. Note a legacy, un-enriched name normalizes to the string `"unknown"` instead; see the consumer requirements below. Tightening this from false to true is a BREAKING change for anything downstream that gates on it.

secret.description: Whether the value is sensitive and must be masked in any UI. Defaults to TRUE, deliberately fail-safe: a declared variable is assumed sensitive until an author says otherwise. Set it to false for a path, a base URL, or an account id.

format.description: Input-shape hint for a guided-setup UI. An OPEN vocabulary — this list is expected to grow, and an unrecognised value degrades the record rather than dropping it. Never an enforcement: Trinity does not validate the credential's value against it.

setup_url.description: Where an operator goes to obtain this credential — typically the vendor's console. MUST be https, MUST have a host, and MUST NOT carry userinfo: `https://google.com@evil.tld/apikey` renders as one host and resolves to another, and this link appears beside a 'paste your API key' prompt. Known residual, not claimed closed: an IDN homograph host is printable and survives validation, so a consumer MUST render the parsed hostname next to the link rather than only the anchor text.

default.description: A safe, non-secret default a UI may pre-fill, e.g. "./Brain" for a vault path. NEVER put a real credential here — template.yaml is committed to the repo.

^x-.description: Vendor extension escape hatch. Any `x-`-prefixed key is ignored by Trinity and never reported as an unknown key. Everything else is a named error with a 'did you mean' suggestion, because silently ignoring an `is_required:` typo would flip the field's meaning without telling anyone.

$comment: CONSUMER REQUIREMENTS for the normalized records `template_service` emits (each has name, title, description, required, secret, format, setup_url, default, source, platform_injected). (1) A record with `required: "unknown"` carries NO authorial intent — a consumer MUST NOT present it as a required field. Without this, a naive UI renders a seeded agent as five mandatory rows, three of them platform variables nobody can fill and the rest masked password inputs over two filesystem paths. (2) A record with `platform_injected: true` is set by Trinity on the container at creation — a consumer MUST NOT ask an operator to supply it. This is also why the catalog's `required_credentials` count excludes them. (3) `secret: true` (the default) MUST be honoured by masking the input. (4) Author-supplied strings arrive already stripped of non-printable characters and length-capped, but they remain UNTRUSTED text: escape them, and never render `setup_url` as anything but a link whose parsed hostname is also shown. (5) There is intentionally NO reverse cross-reference requirement: a declared variable with no `credential_setup:` entry is normal, not an error — it is a curation signal at most. AUTHORING NOTE: declaring a variable in `credentials:` is a separate edit from referencing it as `${VAR}` in .mcp.json.template, and the compatibility gate T-015 checks the two agree. That is deliberate — .mcp.json.template must not become a second declaration authority — but it is real author cost, so seed `credentials:` from your .mcp.json.template first and enrich second. Two brace forms are NOT visible to Trinity's ${VAR} readers and must not be relied on: `${my-key}` (hyphen) and `${VAR:-default}` (the default form is mis-substituted to an empty string).
